md: Memory-resident code trades persistence for stealth. The defender's answer is to capture memory before anyone reboots, restarts a service or "cleans" the host, and to treat the image as the only copy of that evidence.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it
md: Scope by exposure, not only by proof of theft. Every account with a session or cached logon on a compromised host goes on the reset list. Memory adds who touched LSASS and how, which tells you whether the attacker could also have reached accounts that were not logged on.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: Separate policy from mechanism. Good policies (address-ordered first fit, best fit, segregated fit approximating best fit) gave near-zero fragmentation on real traces once implementation overheads were removed. The remaining job is to implement such a policy fast, which is what size-classed allocators do.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: Start from the happens-before edges your algorithm needs, then pick the weakest ordering that creates each one. Mara Bos suggests treating SeqCst as a warning sign in review: it claims dependence on the order of every SeqCst operation in the program, which is much harder to verify than a single Release/Acquire pair.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU readers pay almost nothing; updaters copy, publish with one pointer store, and defer the free until a grace period has elapsed. A grace period waits only for readers that started before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Off-by-one: a single byte too far
md: Off-by-one bugs live at the boundary. A test suite that tries length n - 1, n and n + 1 for every buffer finds most of them; AddressSanitizer turns the silent one-byte write into a loud error.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: A triplet only produces gradient when the negative is inside d(a,p) + m. Mining decides which of those active triplets you spend compute on.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
md: Misconception: "overlapping intervals prove the versions are equal". They show you could not detect a difference at this noise level. A smaller real difference may exist; to find it, reduce noise or take more runs.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
md: Fully async makes training **off-policy**: the trainer learns from groups generated under older weights. The docs recommend staying synchronous while you debug a recipe or validate loss and reward code, where an exact on-policy cadence matters more than throughput.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Read the case study's reward numbers the way the report does: the nine-step moving average rose from 0.438 to 0.556 over 100 steps, but one run on one task set cannot separate that from run-to-run variation, so it is an observation, not a measured improvement.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model
md: Treat everything inside the app as readable and changeable by its user. The app's job is to protect the user's data from *other* parties (other apps, thieves, the network). Decisions about what a user is allowed to do belong on the server.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
md: A WebView bridge turns 'which page is loaded' into 'who can call our native code'. Control both: what may load, and which origin each bridge call came from.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
md: This argument explains the *direction* of a single step, with moving averages switched off. It says nothing about momentum: Bernstein and Newhouse treat the averages as smoothing against mini-batch noise, and call their exact role an open question. Muon adds momentum for empirical reasons.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Choosing an optimizer: how much faster is it really?
md: An optimizer claim is only as good as its baseline. Ask: was the baseline tuned as hard, at more than one scale and data ratio, compared at the end of training, and in which unit (steps, tokens, FLOPs or hours)? Independent tests put matrix optimizers ahead of AdamW, by less than first reported.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
md: One rule generates muP: every weight and every update should have spectral norm about the square root of fan_out over fan_in. For Adam that means learning rate 1/fan_in for every layer; for SGD, fan_out/fan_in.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC trades space for concurrency: every update leaves an old version behind so that readers already in flight can keep a consistent view without blocking writers.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
md: MVCC moves the cost of concurrency into the storage engine: dead versions to clean, index entries to maintain, and XIDs to freeze. Long-lived snapshots make all three worse.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
md: The gates are independent sigmoids, not a softmax. They do not have to sum to 1, so the model can turn several branches up or down at once. Also note what NSA does *not* do: it keeps the full KV cache (and three branches with independent keys and values), so it cuts the bytes *read* per step, not the bytes *stored*.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
md: MIH is fast only when substring buckets stay small. Norouzi et al. analyze uniformly distributed codes and find a substring length of about log2 of the database size works well. Highly skewed hashes (many near-blank images with the same hash) create giant buckets. PDQ's quality score, a 0 to 100 measure of how much detail an image has (next lesson), flags such featureless images so they can be filtered out.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running for real: metrics, checkpoints, export and a multi-node recipe
md: In all three published runs generation takes about half the step or more. Read your own `timing/train/` split before tuning: if generation dominates, the levers are vLLM parallelism and memory (lesson 4), non-colocated async generation (lesson 5) and response length, not the training backend.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
md: Address-based trust is the real bug behind classic hijacking. Any system that grants access because a packet claims a source IP (old rsh, IP allow lists alone, zone transfers allowed by address) is relying on something an attacker can forge. Use cryptographic authentication.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: From overview to stream: the Wireshark workflow, decryption and tshark
md: A key log file is the key to every session it lists. Treat it like a password file: create it only for test traffic on your own machine, store it with the capture under the same protection, and delete both when done. Never set SSLKEYLOGFILE on a machine others use.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
md: A hash lookup that returns nothing does not mean a file is safe: new and targeted malware is unknown by definition. Treat unknown executables from unusual sources as suspicious until analysed.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
md: Routing is decided hop by hop from tables, and the most specific matching prefix wins. On the internet those tables are built from announcements other networks make, which BGP accepts on trust unless someone filters or validates them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: Reading is not touching. The `mbind(2)` man page notes that a first *read* of an anonymous page maps a shared page of zeros held by the kernel; no page is allocated on your node until the first *write*. A warm-up loop that only reads does not place anything.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
md: A drive does not know which LBAs your file system considers free. Unless told (lesson 4), every LBA ever written counts as live. Agrawal et al. put it bluntly: unlike a log-structured file system (one that, like an FTL, appends every write to a log and cleans it, but knows which files were deleted), the disk here is always full, so cleaning pressure is maximal all the time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: AP measures ranking quality across all thresholds for one class; COCO mAP averages it over 10 IoU thresholds and all classes. When comparing papers, check which one is reported: AP50 and AP@[.5:.95] differ a lot for the same model.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
md: Tiered storage moves *old* data to S3 and leaves the write path alone. S3-native moves the *write path itself* to S3, trading commit latency for stateless compute. Hybrids like Neon put a small quorum log in front so commits stay fast while object storage holds the bulk.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: Alert on symptoms, not causes. The SRE book's advice is to focus much more effort on catching symptoms than causes, and to worry about a cause only when it is very definite and very imminent. A page saying "cache hit rate dropped" is a cause; a page saying "users are burning the checkout budget at 20x" is a symptom, and it stays correct when the cause next time is something else.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Layout-aware models add *where* to *what*: each word's box becomes embedding lookups, so a model can learn that a value sits right of its key. OCR-free models fold reading into the network and emit structure directly.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Linux capabilities: splitting root into pieces
md: `docker run --privileged` gives the container all capabilities and access to all host devices (Docker documentation). Treat it as running the workload as root on the host. The same goes for adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_SYS_MODULE` "just for one feature".

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
md: Red lines in this course: no locating, profiling or tracking of specific private individuals; no misrepresentation to get access; no use of credentials or data from breaches; no publishing of personal details. Worked examples use your own organisation, a fictional company (Northwind, under the reserved `.example` domain) or public institutions and already-public cases.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Metadata: what photos and documents say about themselves
md: Files describe themselves. Read metadata as one clue that needs corroboration; remove it from everything you publish.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
md: Check only your own accounts, or colleagues' with their consent. Looking up someone else's email in breach data or a broker profile, without a lawful basis, is exactly the profiling this course rules out.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: A cache hit needs the whole prefix up to a block boundary to match. Chained hashes make that a sequence of dictionary lookups, and keeping freed blocks cached until they are actually reallocated makes eviction LRU for free.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
md: What defenders take from 2022: young algorithms can fail completely, and to classical math. Hence three habits used throughout this course: **hybrids** during the transition (security holds if either component does), **diversity** (HQC as a backup on different math; SLH-DSA relying only on hashes) and **crypto agility**, so that replacing an algorithm is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Database textbooks sometimes say a filter is *highly selective* when it keeps very few rows, the opposite direction to the ratio. When reading docs, check whether they mean the ratio $s$ or the strictness. Here, small $s$ always means few matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
md: **Prefetching is a way to raise concurrency.** A prefetch is a miss started early, before the program's own load. Anything that lets more independent misses overlap (prefetchers, unrolled loops, several independent lists walked at once, more threads) moves you up the curve.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Sparse data: how a few ratings re-identified Netflix users
md: In sparse, high-dimensional data, every person is an outlier. A handful of rare facts, even noisy ones, is enough to find a record, and then the whole record is exposed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Never let users re-run a noisy query for free. Repeated noisy answers can be averaged; composition counts every one. Cache answers or charge each run to the budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
md: Do not treat LINDDUN as a compliance checklist. Its value is the same as STRIDE's: asking each element and flow "how could this hurt the people in the data?" before the design is fixed.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise
md: A privacy review asks, in order: what data actions happen, how they could hurt people (LINDDUN), whether the processing is necessary (DPIA), what must leave the system and the matching technique (DP, PSI, secure aggregation, or not releasing), how the design minimises, and how rights reach every copy.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: A correct final answer does not mean correct reasoning. On GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021: about 8,500 grade-school math word problems), Uesato et al. found that RL directly against final-answer correctness left a best **trace error** (any human-judged mistake in the reasoning, among answer-correct solutions) of 12.4%, versus 3.8% for their best process-based method.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Who runs next: run queues, CFS, EEVDF and nice
md: Linux runs, on each CPU, a task that has not had more than its weighted fair share: CFS picks the smallest vruntime; EEVDF picks, among eligible tasks (lag of zero or more), the earliest virtual deadline. Nice values set weights 1.25x apart; slices end on ticks and wakeups, and those are your involuntary switches.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Self-consistency grades a generator with a predictor that was trained on natural proteins, and both can be wrong in the same direction. A design that AF2 loves is not proven to fold: it has passed one cheap filter. Everything after this point costs money and weeks.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Reading CSV exports and JSON records without breaking them
md: Never split CSV or JSON by hand. `csv.DictReader` and `json.loads` implement the quoting and escaping rules you would otherwise get wrong, and wrong parsing in security tooling means missed indicators.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Vocabulary mismatch: why BM25 misses relevant documents
md: Better scoring cannot fix a zero-overlap miss. Query expansion changes **which documents can match at all** by adding terms to the query (or, in document expansion, to the documents). That is a recall tool first, and every added term is also a new way to match the wrong document.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
md: Misconception: rewriting is free accuracy. Besides latency and cost, a rewriter can **drift** from the user's intent (RAG-Fusion's evaluation saw off-topic answers from unrelated generated queries) and it is a new failure point (timeouts, malformed output). Keep the original query as a fallback or as one of the queries, and log every rewrite next to the original so you can audit drift.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
md: Misconception: "we validate all input, so we are safe". Format checks (is it an integer, is it a known product) do not test meaning (is this quantity possible, is this step allowed now, has this coupon been used). Logic flaws live in the meaning.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Starbucks gift cards and two browser sessions (2015)
md: Protect the resource being spent, not the path to it. A one-time flag in the session, a disabled button or a cleared form all guard one route to the balance; a lock or atomic update on the balance itself guards every route.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Testing logic: invariants, abuse cases and concurrency tests
md: Write the invariant first, then a test that tries to break it in every way this course showed: odd values, odd order, and many at once. A test suite with no parallel test cannot fail on a race.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
md: Consensus is safe without any timing assumptions; timing only buys availability. Every production feature here (reads, reconfiguration, Pre-Vote) is checked against the same question: can two majorities that do not overlap make conflicting decisions?

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: Shape raw signals before the model sees them: turn age into a decaying freshness, counts into logs or rates, and remember that query-only features can only matter through interactions.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
md: Compare systems on per-query differences, with a paired t-test or randomization test, and report the mean difference with a confidence interval and effect size. With many systems, control the familywise error instead of running dozens of independent tests.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
md: Joining hypervisors, backup servers and RMM consoles to the production domain feels tidy, but it gives whoever owns AD the keys to everything at once. Separate authentication for these systems is the single design choice that most often decides whether a domain compromise becomes a business-ending outage.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
md: Every reward-side fix encodes an assumption about *where* the reward is wrong: in members' disagreement, in label noise, in a named feature, or in extreme values. Hacks that live outside that assumption pass straight through, so these methods complement an outside check; they do not replace it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: Multiplying ordinal numbers (ranks, like 1 to 5) treats the gap between 4 and 5 as equal to the gap between 1 and 2, which is rarely true of real losses. Grids are fine for sorting a long list quickly and for talking to non-specialists. They are not fine for deciding whether a USD 300,000 control is worth buying. For that, estimate in money.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: Misconception: "we implemented the CSF". The CSF lists outcomes, not controls; you cannot install it. Saying you *use* it means you have profiles, owners for the gaps and a review cycle. A slide with the six function names is not alignment.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
md: A control that runs as code on every change is both stronger security and better evidence: the CI logs show it ran on every pull request all year, and the evidence store shows the state on any date an auditor picks. Failing the build is the cheapest moment to fix a compliance gap.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
md: Cyber insurance transfers part of the financial tail: forensics, restoration, business interruption, liability. It is priced and conditioned on your controls; misstatements can void claims. Model deductible and limit against your loss distribution, read the exclusions (fraud, war and state-backed attacks), and keep the application as true as your SOC 2.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Variable-length sequences on the trainer: packing and balance
md: Variable lengths waste trainer compute three ways: padding inside a row, empty rows, and idle ranks. Pack rows (with `cu_seqlens`), balance tokens across ranks, and normalize the loss by the global token count so none of this changes the gradient.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100, NVIDIA's 2017 data center GPU (125 TFLOP/s of Tensor Core math over about 900 GB/s, a ridge of 138.9), to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask (the set of CPUs a task may run on, set with `sched_setaffinity()`).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: Misconception: once a task is in a custom DSQ it is on its way to a CPU. It is in your custody until dispatch moves it, and a property change can pull it back out through `ops.dequeue()` at any time.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Vaults: one place to store, control and audit secrets
md: A vault concentrates risk. CircleCI was, in effect, a vault for its customers' deploy secrets. Narrow policies per workload, short-lived tokens, audit logs shipped elsewhere, the ability to seal fast, and a root of trust in a KMS or HSM are what make the concentration worth it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
md: Trace by hand: mark the source, follow every assignment and call, and stop at each sink. A function only counts as a sanitizer if its output is safe for that specific sink, whatever the input. Rewriting or deleting bad patterns almost never qualifies.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
md: Parameterising user data protects you only if the component never interprets the final string. When reviewing a feature that adds interpretation (lookups, templates, expressions, fetching URLs) to a widely used API, treat every caller's data as reaching that new sink.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
md: Memory-safety policy is now a review topic: new memory-unsafe code needs a reason, unsafe blocks in Rust get the most scrutiny, and old C and C++ keeps its hardening. Android's data says the payoff comes from new code, because vulnerabilities concentrate in recent changes.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
md: Everything in the KEXINIT lists is negotiated in the clear and only later authenticated through the exchange hash. Anything the hash does not cover (extra messages, the implicit sequence numbers) is a place where an active attacker can interfere.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
md: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Integrity: no read down, no write up. If you remember which way information is allowed to flow, you can rebuild both rule sets.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
md: A proxy only protects an application if it is the only way in and the application can tell the difference. Signed, audience-bound assertions let the application check for itself.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
md: Pace all workers with one shared limiter, honour Retry-After and the reset headers, back off exponentially with full jitter, retry only idempotent calls and only at one layer, and report partial failures item by item.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: A hash only proves integrity if the expected fingerprint reached you over a channel the attacker cannot touch. If an attacker can change both the message and the published hash, the check passes. Fixing that needs authenticity: a digital signature (or a keyed hash) that only the real sender can produce. The cryptography course covers these.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
md: CVSS = how bad in theory. KEV = being used now. EPSS = likely to be used soon. Combine them with what *your* asset is and how exposed it is. A score without context is not a priority.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Rules of thumb that keep you on the right side: test only systems you own or have written permission to test; stay inside the agreed scope (systems, dates, methods); stop and report the moment you see other people's data; never keep or share it. A bug bounty programme's published rules are a form of written permission, but only for what they list.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Budgets: what security costs and how to ask for money
md: Weak argument: "the average breach costs USD 4.99 million, so give us 1 million." The average is not your loss, the board knows it, and the request names no risk and no result. Strong argument: "this USD 250k removes an estimated 700k of expected annual loss from ransomware on our order system, according to our FAIR model with these ranges."

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: The operating model: decision rights, incentives and culture
md: Write down who decides (one Accountable per activity), make the secure way the easy way, give teams a clear intake with service levels, and align incentives with security outcomes. Culture shows in which priority wins when they conflict.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides
md: Do not soften the verdict to keep a client happy, and do not dramatise it to be noticed. Both destroy the summary's main asset: that the reader can take it at face value. If the news is good, say so plainly; a calibrated "the defences held" is as useful as a warning.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: A common misconception: self-play means no external signal. Games have a perfect, free judge: the rules decide who won. Take that away and a model playing against itself only amplifies its own beliefs, which is the collapse setting from the prerequisite course.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
md: Each method buys information somewhere. V-STaR gets more out of the answer key by learning from failures; SCoRe uses the answer key to reward fixes; Meta-Rewarding has no outside signal, so it can only exploit its own generation-verification gap, which Song et al. saw shrink to about zero within a few rounds on math.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Evaluate compression like a model change: measure your task metric at several ratios on your own data, and measure end-to-end latency including the compressor. The published gains were measured on specific benchmarks with specific target models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Equifax and Spring4Shell: when the framework evaluates input
md: Equifax, Spring4Shell, ProxyLogon (lesson 14) and MOVEit all ended the same way: a **web shell** written into a directory the web server executes. Two cheap controls hit all of them: make web roots read-only to the app's own user, and alert on new script files appearing there.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Prefix reuse is a property of the *whole serving path*: frontend hints, the radix tree, queue order on each worker, and routing across workers. Each layer can preserve reuse or destroy it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Two ceilings limit SIMD: latency chains (fix with several independent accumulators) and memory bandwidth (fix by doing more work per byte or keeping data in cache). Lane count only matters once both are out of the way.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Low-precision rollout: FP8 weights, FP8 KV cache and INT4
md: INT4 checkpoints use a `compressed-tensors` config whose `ignore` list also steers online quantization. The debug guide's example: if the MoE router `mlp.gate.weight` is not ignored, slime INT4-quantizes it, SGLang does not expect quantized names for the router and silently skips them, and the router weights end up all zeros. `--check-weight-update-equal` (lesson 3) catches this.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering
md: slime treats SGLang as a behavior policy q. TIS caps the correction, IcePop drops out-of-band tokens, R3 removes MoE routing flips at the source, and score centering repairs the baseline. All need rollout log probs on every sample, and all are judged by the same few metrics.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Inside the EVM: storage, calls, msg.sender and delegatecall
md: CALL: their code, their storage. DELEGATECALL: their code, **your** storage and your money. Treat every delegatecall target as if it were your own code, because in effect it is.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
md: Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
md: Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
md: Misconception: "it's only dangerous if someone opens a file on the drive". Devices that present themselves as a keyboard can type commands as soon as they are connected, and a network implant needs no user action at all. Controls must act at connection time.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
md: A working SAE pipeline is: cache a site with BOS dropped, shuffle, normalise by one scalar, train with transposed init and unit decoder columns (plus AuxK at scale), then judge it by L0, FVU and delta LM loss from splicing. A released SAE plus Neuronpedia gets you to reading and steering in a few lines.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf stat -e page-faults,major-faults`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
md: Steering is a research and monitoring tool before it is a product control. Use it when you need to know *which* internal direction drives a behavior, to detect a concept, or to add to a prompt (CAA's vectors still moved behavior on top of system prompts). Always report per-input effects, a random vector of equal norm and a prompting baseline; without them a mean effect proves little.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
md: The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: The derivative is not the change in $f$ over a big step. It is a rate at one point. For $x^2$ at 3, a step of $+2$ actually raises $f$ by 16, not $6 \times 2 = 12$, because the slope itself changes along the way. This is exactly why **gradient descent**, the training method that repeatedly moves every parameter a small step downhill (lesson 6), takes small steps.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
md: Multiply local derivatives along each path, then add over all paths from the input to the output. Fan-out in the forward pass becomes a sum in the backward pass.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: A mode is nine bits in three groups of rwx (owner, group, others), written as three octal digits with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. On a file, x means run it; on a directory, x means enter it. Exactly one group applies to you.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: `sed -i` edits a file in place, and it differs between systems. GNU sed (Linux) takes an optional backup suffix glued to the flag, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` works. BSD sed (macOS) requires the suffix argument, so the same command takes the script as the suffix and fails. `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' f` works on both and keeps the original as `f.bak`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, other interactive shells ~/.bashrc, scripts neither. ssh logs you in with a key pair whose private half never leaves your machine, and tmux keeps remote work alive when the connection drops.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
md: Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization
md: Decode time per token is about weight bytes over bandwidth, so halving bits per weight roughly halves it. Weight-only quantization cuts bytes, not FLOPs: it speeds decode, not prefill.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Measure it: tokens per second, MBU and MFU
md: Compare every measurement with its floor. MBU near 70 to 80% at small batch means the bytes are the limit, so cut bytes (quantize) or add bandwidth (tensor parallelism). MBU far lower means overhead: launches, Python, unfused kernels.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: Misconception: "the CPU knows whether a value is signed." It does not. `cmp` sets all four flags every time; the signedness lives only in which jump the compiler chose after it.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: C is small: a handful of types, operators that work on bits and integers as directly as the CPU does, and `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` and functions. What makes it hard is not syntax but the rules for memory, which the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: `void *` carries an address without a type; the code that receives it must convert it back to the right type. A function pointer carries code. Together they let one function such as qsort work on any data, with the caller supplying the type-specific part.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation: a held-out split used for tuning, see lesson 8) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes that Windows NTFS and SGI's XFS use forms of it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Accumulation is exactly equivalent only for layers that treat examples independently. **BatchNorm** computes statistics per micro-batch: with examples (1, 2, 3, 4) in one batch it normalizes the value 2 to -0.45, but in the micro-batch (1, 2) it becomes +1.00. The playbook also notes that accumulation gives no throughput benefit, since it runs the same small batches; it only changes the effective batch size.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
md: Reproducible builds prove the binary matches *the source you built from*. They say nothing about which source that should be. xz 5.6.1's release tarball contained a malicious build script missing from git; rebuilding the tarball reproduces the backdoor perfectly. Compare release archives against the tagged git tree too (Arch Linux switched xz to building from git when the backdoor was disclosed).

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
md: The successors keep the frame (a memory trained on a key-value loss as the sequence streams) and change what it fits and how well. A window or an exact solve protects earlier writes; a robust loss protects against outliers; forgetting decides how fast a changed fact wins. None of it is settled at scale.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
md: Both frameworks end the same way: a hunt is finished when its results are documented and handed to the teams that act on them. The query is not the deliverable. The deliverables are an escalation (if needed), detections, data and security recommendations, and knowledge for the next hunt.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements
md: The most common failure is a collection-driven programme: buy feeds, read everything, publish a weekly "threat landscape" digest that supports no decision. FIRST warns that a meeting with leadership that is "informational only" will not go well. Start from requirements and work backwards.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
md: Weigh evidence by how well it *discriminates* between hypotheses, not by how much of it agrees with your favourite. Look for the item that would disprove each hypothesis, check its sensitivity, and always keep "someone wants us to think this" on the list.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
md: The numbers are estimates and the tree is never complete. Schneier calls the safe example incomplete and warns not to read its values as a statement about how secure a real safe is. Use trees to compare options and find the cheapest path, not to claim an attack costs exactly 2,200.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
md: Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
md: "We revoked the certificate, so we are safe" is wishful thinking. Revocation reaches clients slowly and unreliably. Assume a compromised certificate is usable until it expires, and size your lifetimes accordingly.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
md: Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 study by the security firm NCC Group of two other unikernels, Rumprun and IncludeOS, found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries (a random value placed before a function's return address and checked on return, so a buffer overflow is caught) absent or broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through the V1 trainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. verl's GSM8K example page says the scorer gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0 (the quickstart page also says 0.0). A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: I/O virtualization: emulation, virtio, passthrough and the IOMMU
md: EPT/NPT confines what the guest's *CPU* can touch; the IOMMU confines what the guest's *devices* can touch. Device assignment without an IOMMU (or with a group shared across tenants) quietly removes the memory wall from lesson 3.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Confidential VMs: SEV-SNP, TDX and Arm CCA stop trusting the host
md: A confidential VM moves trust from the host's software to the CPU vendor's hardware and firmware. It protects memory and registers from a curious or compromised host, not availability, not the guest's own bugs, and not data the guest sends through shared pages unencrypted.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
